title: Statistics for Data Analysis
summary: A grounded first course in describing data and reasoning with probability — from charts and averages to distributions and the central limit theorem.
description:
This course builds the statistical vocabulary that every later analysis depends on. Participants start by classifying variables and choosing suitable graphs, then move on to summarising data with measures of central tendency, dispersion, skewness and kurtosis, and to describing the relationship between two variables with correlation and a least-squares line.

The second half introduces probability as the language of uncertainty: sample spaces and events, conditional probability and Bayes' theorem, random variables, expectation and variance, and the binomial, Poisson and normal distributions. It closes with the central limit theorem, which explains why the normal distribution appears so often in practice and prepares participants for inference.
learning_objectives: Classify variables and choose an appropriate chart for categorical and quantitative data
Compute and interpret measures of central tendency, dispersion, skewness and kurtosis
Measure association using Pearson's product-moment and Spearman's rank correlation and fit a least-squares line
Apply conditional probability and Bayes' theorem to simple decision problems
Work with discrete and continuous random variables, expectation, variance and moment generating functions
Use the binomial, Poisson and normal distributions and explain the role of the central limit theorem

title: Statistical Inference & Hypothesis Testing
summary: Learn how to estimate unknown quantities and test claims from sample data — from maximum likelihood to t, chi-square, F tests and ANOVA.
description:
Statistical inference is the step from describing a sample to drawing conclusions about a population. This course covers what makes a good estimator, how to build point and interval estimates, and how maximum likelihood estimation works. It then sets out the logic of hypothesis testing: null and alternative hypotheses, critical regions, significance levels, one- and two-tailed tests, the two types of error and the Neyman–Pearson lemma.

Participants apply this framework to large-sample tests for means and proportions, small-sample t and F tests, chi-square tests for goodness of fit and independence, and one-way and two-way analysis of variance. A short module on nonparametric checks — the runs test for randomness and the one-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test — rounds out the toolkit for situations where distributional assumptions are doubtful.
learning_objectives: Distinguish parameters from statistics and explain sampling distributions and standard errors
Evaluate estimators for unbiasedness, efficiency, consistency and sufficiency, and derive maximum likelihood estimates
Formulate hypotheses, choose a significance level and interpret Type I and Type II errors
Carry out large-sample, t, F and chi-square tests and construct the related confidence intervals
Analyse one-way and two-way classified data with ANOVA
Apply the runs test and one-sample Kolmogorov–Smirnov test when parametric assumptions are questionable

title: Excel for Data Analytics
summary: A practical spreadsheet course covering data import and cleaning, lookups, logical and statistical functions, PivotTables and charts.
description:
Spreadsheets remain the most widely used analysis tool in many organisations. This short course takes participants from basic formulas to confident analytical work in Excel: bringing data in from text files and the web, splitting and de-duplicating it, and writing formulas that copy correctly using absolute and relative references.

Participants then build logical tests with IF, nested IF, AND, OR and NOT, summarise data with SUMIF, COUNTIF and related statistical functions, retrieve values with lookup functions, and summarise large lists with PivotTables and PivotCharts. The course finishes with charting techniques and worksheet formatting so that results are presented clearly.
learning_objectives: Import, clean and restructure data using text-to-columns, duplicate removal and grouping
Write formulas with correct absolute and relative cell references
Use lookup, logical and conditional statistical functions to answer business questions
Summarise and explore data with PivotTables and PivotCharts
Present results with appropriate charts and well-formatted worksheets

title: R Programming for Statistics
summary: Get started with R: objects, data input and output, calculations, plots and descriptive statistics with probability distributions.
description:
R was built for statistical computing, and this short course introduces it from the ground up. Participants learn how R works, how to create, list and delete objects, how to read and write data files, and how to generate regular and random sequences, carry out arithmetic and matrix computations, and manipulate objects.

The second part uses R for statistical work: producing graphics and plots, computing measures of central tendency and frequency distributions, using generic functions, and working with discrete and continuous probability distributions. By the end, participants can take a small dataset from file to summary statistics and charts entirely in R.

Read data from and write data to files
Generate regular and random sequences and perform arithmetic and matrix computations
Produce graphics and plots to explore data
Compute descriptive statistics and frequency distributions

title: Python Programming for Data Science
summary: A beginner's introduction to Python — installing and running programs, debugging, variables, control flow, file input/output and plotting data.
description:
This short course gives newcomers a solid footing in core Python before they move on to analytical work. Participants install Python, run programs interactively and as scripts, and learn to recognise and fix syntax, runtime and semantic errors. They then work with values, types, variables, operators and expressions, and control the flow of a program with conditional statements and loops.

The course ends with practical data handling: reading data from text files, file input and output, and producing simple plots with a Python visualisation library. It deliberately concentrates on programming fundamentals, giving participants the base they need for later data-science and machine-learning courses.

Use values, types, variables, operators and expressions correctly, including type conversion

title: SQL & Databases for Data Science
summary: Design relational databases and query them with SQL — from ER modelling and normalisation to joins, subqueries, window functions, triggers and procedures.
description:
Most organisational data lives in databases, so querying them well is a core analytical skill. This course introduces database management systems and data models, then teaches how to design a database with entity–relationship diagrams and normalise it to third normal form to remove redundancy and anomalies.

Participants then use SQL (with MySQL) to create and alter tables with primary and foreign keys, write queries with filtering, joins, aggregation and GROUP BY, use subqueries and window functions for ordered data, and work with constraints, views, triggers, stored procedures and cursors. The course also covers basic statistics and data munging in SQL, and introduces document and graph databases as alternatives for data science work.

Design a database with ER diagrams and normalise it up to third normal form

title: Data Visualization
summary: Turn data into clear graphics: map data to aesthetics, use colour well, and visualise amounts, distributions, proportions, trends and geospatial data.
description:
Good charts make analysis understandable; poor ones mislead. This course treats visualisation as a set of deliberate design choices. Participants learn how data values are mapped onto aesthetics and scales, how coordinate systems (including nonlinear and curved axes) change what a reader sees, and how to use colour to distinguish groups, represent values and highlight what matters.

The course then works through a directory of chart types — bar, grouped and stacked bars, dot plots and heatmaps for amounts; histograms, empirical cumulative distribution functions and Q-Q plots for distributions; pie charts, side-by-side and stacked bars for proportions; and smoothing, detrending and time-series decomposition for trends — before introducing map projections, layers, choropleths and cartograms for geospatial data. It builds on the basic graphs for categorical and quantitative data used in descriptive statistics.

Use colour to distinguish categories, represent values and highlight key findings
Select appropriate charts for amounts, distributions, proportions and x–y relationships

title: Regression & Predictive Modelling
summary: Build, evaluate and regularise regression models — from least squares and correlation to multiple and polynomial regression, ridge, lasso and logistic regression.
description:
Regression is the workhorse of predictive analysis. This course begins with correlation and the least-squares line, then extends to multiple explanatory variables and polynomial terms. Participants learn to evaluate models properly with cross-validation and other measures, and to control overfitting with regularisation — Tikhonov (ridge) regression and the lasso.

A module on gradient descent shows how models are fitted numerically by minimising the sum of squared errors, including the role of the learning rate and least-mean-squares updates. The course closes with models for a binary outcome: logistic regression and discriminant analysis, and how the two approaches compare in a classification decision.

Build multiple and polynomial regression models and interpret their coefficients
Evaluate models with the coefficient of determination and cross-validation

title: Time Series Analysis & Forecasting
summary: Analyse data recorded over time — trend, seasonality, AR and MA models, exponential smoothing forecasts and index numbers — with hands-on lab work.
description:
Sales, prices, demand and many other business and economic quantities are recorded over time. This course explains how to break a time series into its components using additive and multiplicative models, measure trend by freehand, semi-averages, moving averages and least squares, fit growth curves, and estimate seasonal indices.

Participants then move to Box–Jenkins ideas: moving-average and autoregressive processes of orders one and two, the autocorrelation function as a guide to model order, and estimation of AR(1) and AR(2) parameters with least squares and the Yule–Walker equations. Exponential smoothing provides a practical forecasting method, and a final module covers the construction of simple and weighted index numbers, including Laspeyres, Paasche, Marshall–Edgeworth and Fisher indices, reversal tests and cost-of-living indices.
learning_objectives: Identify trend, seasonal, cyclical and irregular components and choose additive or multiplicative models
Measure trend using moving averages, semi-averages and least squares, and fit growth curves
Compute seasonal indices by simple averages, ratio to moving averages and ratio to trend
Use the ACF to suggest model order and fit AR(1) and AR(2) models via Yule–Walker and least squares
Produce forecasts using exponential smoothing
Construct and test simple and weighted index numbers, including a cost-of-living index

title: Machine Learning Fundamentals
summary: Learn the core ideas and classical algorithms of machine learning — optimisation, regression, trees, ensembles, SVM, naive Bayes, kNN and k-means — with lab implementations.
description:
This course introduces machine learning as the study of systems that learn from data. It begins with types of learning, the steps of an ML workflow, numerical representation issues such as overflow and underflow, and the linear algebra and optimisation ideas — norms, matrix decompositions, constrained and unconstrained optimisation and gradient descent — that algorithms depend on.

Participants then study the learning paradigm through linear regression, goodness of fit, the bias–variance trade-off, variants of gradient descent and maximum likelihood estimation, before working through classical techniques: decision trees, bagging, random forests, gradient boosting, support vector machines, naive Bayes, k-nearest neighbours and k-means. Data pre-processing and feature selection with filters and wrappers are covered so that models are trained on well-prepared inputs. Lab sessions implement these algorithms and evaluate them with accuracy, precision and recall.
learning_objectives: Distinguish supervised and unsupervised learning and outline the steps of a machine-learning project
Prepare data through cleaning, integration, reduction, transformation and feature selection

title: Deep Learning & Advanced Machine Learning
summary: Go beyond classical ML: feedforward and convolutional networks, RNNs and LSTMs, training and regularisation of deep models, ensembles and statistical pattern recognition.
description:
This advanced course covers the neural-network methods behind modern machine learning. It starts with feedforward networks — single and multilayer perceptrons, activation functions, gradient-based learning and back-propagation — and the techniques that make deep models trainable: regularisation and norm penalties, dataset augmentation, early stopping, parameter initialisation, adaptive learning rates and batch normalisation.

Participants then study convolutional networks (convolution, pooling and common architectures, with transfer learning), sequence models (RNNs, bidirectional and deep RNNs, back-propagation through time, LSTM and attention), and applications such as natural language processing and generative adversarial networks. Ensemble methods (stacking, bagging, boosting) and a statistical pattern-recognition module — Bayesian decision theory, kernel and nearest-neighbour methods, Parzen windows and self-organising networks — complete the picture.

title: Multivariate Statistical Analysis
summary: Analyse many variables at once — the multivariate normal model, discriminant analysis, logistic regression, principal components, factor analysis and clustering.
description:
Real datasets rarely involve a single variable. This course provides the methods to explore, model and simplify multivariate data. It begins with mean vectors, dispersion and correlation matrices and graphical displays, then develops the multivariate normal distribution, maximum likelihood estimation of its parameters, tests of linear hypotheses, and partial and multiple correlation.

Participants then learn to classify observations with discriminant analysis and logistic regression, reduce dimension with principal components (including biplots) and the orthogonal factor model, and group observations with cluster analysis based on similarity measures and statistical models. Lab sessions apply each technique to data and include tests for multiple correlation and correlation matrices.
learning_objectives: Summarise multivariate data with mean vectors, dispersion and correlation matrices and graphical displays
Work with the multivariate normal distribution and estimate its parameters
Test hypotheses about multiple and partial correlation and regression coefficients

title: Survival & Reliability Analysis
summary: Model time-to-event data: hazard functions, lifetime distributions, censoring, Kaplan–Meier and Nelson–Aalen estimators, system reliability and queuing applications.
description:
Many questions are about how long until something happens — a component fails, a patient relapses, a customer leaves. This course introduces the survival, hazard, cumulative hazard and reversed hazard functions, increasing and decreasing failure-rate classes and bath-tub shaped hazards, and the lifetime distributions used to model them: exponential, gamma, Weibull, Rayleigh and lognormal.

Participants learn how censoring arises and how to estimate survival with the Kaplan–Meier estimator and cumulative hazard with the Nelson–Aalen estimator, with confidence intervals and Q-Q and hazard plots. Reliability theory covers series, parallel, k-out-of-n and standby systems, and a module on stochastic processes connects Markov chains, Poisson and birth–death processes to reliability and queuing models. Lab work uses SPSS, with R and other statistical packages as alternatives.
learning_objectives: Relate survival, hazard, cumulative hazard and reversed hazard functions to one another
Fit and compare lifetime distributions including exponential, gamma, Weibull, Rayleigh and lognormal
Recognise types of censoring and estimate survival with Kaplan–Meier and cumulative hazard with Nelson–Aalen
Assess fit with Q-Q and hazard plots and construct confidence intervals for survival
Compute reliability of series, parallel, k-out-of-n and standby systems
Use Markov chains, Poisson and birth–death processes to describe simple queuing and reliability problems

title: Experimental Design & Sampling
summary: Plan data collection that answers the question — questionnaires, sample surveys, random, stratified, cluster and systematic sampling, and CRD, RBD, Latin square and factorial designs.
description:
The quality of an analysis is fixed largely at the planning stage. This course covers both ways of gathering data well: surveys and experiments. It starts with primary and secondary data, questionnaire and schedule design, and the principal steps of a sample survey, including sampling frames, sampling units and control of variability.

Participants then study simple random sampling with and without replacement, sampling for proportions, stratified, cluster and systematic sampling, and regression estimators. The experimental-design half covers the basic principles of experimentation and ANOVA, completely randomised, randomised block and Latin square designs (including missing observations and relative efficiency), two- and three-level factorial experiments, fractional factorials and split-plot designs.

Use regression estimators to improve precision in surveys
Apply the principles of randomisation, replication and blocking to experiments
Lay out and analyse CRD, RBD and Latin square designs, including missing observations
Plan and interpret factorial, fractional factorial and split-plot experiments

title: Statistical Quality Control
summary: Monitor and improve processes with control charts and acceptance sampling — X-bar, R, s, p and np charts, ARL, and single and double sampling plans.
description:
Statistical quality control applies statistical methods to keeping products and services within specification. This course places SQC in the wider context of quality improvement and total quality management, including quality costs and the link between quality and productivity.

Participants learn the statistical basis of control charts — chance versus assignable causes, choice of control and warning limits, rational subgroups, sample size and frequency, pattern analysis and average run length — and construct 3-sigma charts for variables (X-bar and R, X-bar and s) and attributes (p and np). The final module covers acceptance sampling with single and double sampling plans and their OC and ASN functions.

Distinguish chance and assignable causes and set control and warning limits
Construct and interpret X-bar and R, X-bar and s, p and np charts

Design single and double sampling plans and interpret OC and ASN curves

title: Big Data Analytics with Hadoop & Spark
summary: Store and process large datasets with HDFS, MapReduce, Pig, Hive and Spark, and get introduced to NoSQL stores such as MongoDB and Cassandra.
description:
When data outgrows a single machine, different tools are needed. This course explains the characteristics of big data, why conventional processing falls short, and how big-data frameworks are used across marketing, retail, hospitality and other sectors. It introduces cloud computing and the Hadoop ecosystem: HDFS, cluster architecture and modes, the Hadoop daemons, schedulers, cluster setup, configuration and administration.

Participants write MapReduce programs — word count, matrix multiplication, sorting, indexing, combiners and map-side and reduce-side joins — and follow a MapReduce job through its phases. They then use Pig Latin and Hive for higher-level data processing, build and run Spark applications with RDDs and Spark SQL, create a simple data pipeline with PySpark and Hive, and are introduced to NoSQL storage with MongoDB and Cassandra.

title: Business Analytics & Data Mining
summary: Connect data to decisions: business intelligence, the analytics process, data preparation, data warehousing, association rules, classification and clustering.
description:
This course shows how organisations turn raw data into timely decisions. It begins with the data-science process, the relationship between business intelligence and data science, and the architecture of a business-intelligence system, including the role of mathematical models. Participants then follow the analytics process — descriptive, predictive and prescriptive techniques, plus social-media and behavioural analytics.

The data-mining half covers data preparation (cleaning missing and noisy data, integration, transformation, validation, standardisation and feature extraction), concept description and class comparison, association rule mining and text mining, and clustering with partitioning, hierarchical and density-based methods. A data-warehousing module explains multidimensional models, data cubes, star, snowflake and fact-constellation schemas, and three-tier architecture.

title: Operations Research & Decision Modelling
summary: Model and optimise decisions: linear programming and simplex, duality, transportation and assignment, game theory, decision analysis under risk, simulation and fuzzy decision making.
description:
Operations research provides mathematical tools for allocating scarce resources and choosing between alternatives. This course covers formulating linear programmes and solving them graphically and with the simplex, Big-M, two-phase and dual simplex methods, together with duality theory. Transportation and assignment problems are solved with the north-west corner, least-cost and Vogel's methods, the MODI test and the Hungarian method.

The decision-modelling half introduces payoff matrices, decision making under risk, the value of information, decision trees and Bayesian decisions with experimentation. Game theory runs from two-person zero-sum games and saddle points to Nash equilibrium. Monte-Carlo and discrete-event simulation with pseudo-random numbers handle uncertainty, and a short module on fuzzy multicriteria decision making and fuzzy linear programming addresses imprecise objectives.
learning_objectives: Formulate linear programming models for production, distribution and similar problems
Solve LPs with graphical, simplex, Big-M, two-phase and dual simplex methods and interpret dual values
Solve transportation and assignment problems and test for optimality
Structure decisions with payoff matrices and decision trees and compute the value of information
Analyse two-person zero-sum and non-cooperative games
Use Monte-Carlo simulation and fuzzy linear programming to support decisions under uncertainty

title: Mathematics for Data Science
summary: The linear algebra, calculus, matrix computation, numerical methods and probability inequalities that sit underneath statistics and machine learning.
description:
Data-science methods are built on a small number of mathematical ideas. This course gathers them in one place. The linear-algebra modules cover solving linear systems by Gaussian and Gauss–Jordan elimination, vector spaces, bases and dimension, linear transformations and rank–nullity, inner products, Gram–Schmidt orthonormalisation and eigenvalues — then move to computational practice with LU, Cholesky and QR factorisations, least-squares problems, the singular value decomposition and eigenvalue algorithms such as the power method and QR algorithm.

The calculus module covers limits, continuity, partial differentiation, Jacobians, Taylor series and maxima and minima of functions of two variables, plus multiple integrals for areas and volumes. Numerical methods address errors, root finding, interpolation, numerical differentiation and integration, and iterative solvers. A final module on concentration inequalities — Markov, Chebyshev and Chernoff–Hoeffding — explains why sampling and estimation work. Labs use MATLAB, Mathematica and Excel.
learning_objectives: Solve systems of linear equations and reason about rank, basis, dimension and linear transformations
Compute and apply LU, Cholesky, QR, eigenvalue and singular value decompositions
Use partial derivatives, Taylor expansions and multiple integrals in optimisation and modelling
Apply numerical methods for root finding, interpolation, differentiation, integration and linear systems, and assess their errors
Use Markov, Chebyshev and Chernoff–Hoeffding inequalities to bound estimation error
Carry out matrix and calculus computations in MATLAB, Mathematica or Excel

title: Mathematical Modelling with Differential Equations
summary: Build and solve models of change — first- and second-order ODEs, systems of equations, solution in MATLAB, and simulation models including Monte-Carlo.
description:
Differential equations describe how quantities change, and they underpin models in engineering, the sciences and economics. This course covers the order, degree and geometric meaning of differential equations; exact equations and integrating factors; Clairaut's equation and singular solutions; orthogonal trajectories; and linear equations with constant coefficients, including Cauchy's equation.

Participants then solve second-order linear equations with variable coefficients by reduction to normal form, change of variables and variation of parameters, and handle simultaneous equations. Lab sessions solve these problems in MATLAB using dsolve. The course places this work in a modelling context — theoretical and empirical models, model evaluation and limitations, the steps of a simulation study and validation — and introduces Monte-Carlo simulation with pseudo-random numbers.
learning_objectives: Classify differential equations by order, degree and linearity and interpret them geometrically
Solve exact, linear, homogeneous and Bernoulli first-order equations
Solve second-order linear equations using constant-coefficient methods and variation of parameters
Solve simultaneous differential equations analytically and with MATLAB's dsolve

Set up a simple Monte-Carlo simulation using pseudo-random numbers

title: Research Methodology & LaTeX
summary: Plan research properly and write it up professionally — research design, literature review, models and simulation, then LaTeX documents, Beamer slides and BibTeX references.
description:
This course supports students and researchers through two parts of a project that are often learned informally: designing the research and presenting it. The research-methodology part covers types of research, the research process, identifying a topic, defining the problem, conducting a literature survey and review, and research design, along with an introduction to mathematical and simulation models and their validation.

The LaTeX part teaches participants to install and use LaTeX, structure documents with article and book classes, control page layout, format text, write complex mathematics, build tables and insert images, and read error messages. It finishes with presentations in Beamer and bibliography management with BibTeX.

title: Financial Mathematics & Mathematical Economics
summary: The mathematics of interest, discounting and payment series, plus optimisation, linear programming, input–output analysis and game theory applied to economic problems.
description:
This course brings together two applied areas. The financial-mathematics part covers progressions, growth and decay curves, interest rates, the time value of money, simple discount, discrete compounding, and equal-payment, arithmetic-gradient and geometric-gradient series. The economics part applies the same quantitative thinking to production functions (including Cobb–Douglas), returns to scale, marginal cost and revenue, and output decisions under competition and monopoly.

Participants also study optimisation methods in economic analysis, linear and non-linear programming with production and diet problems, Leontief-style input–output analysis with the Hawkins–Simon conditions, game theory, and difference and differential equations in economic dynamics. The course is educational and does not constitute investment or financial advice.

Evaluate equal-payment, gradient and geometric-gradient series with discrete compounding
Analyse production with one and two variable inputs, including Cobb–Douglas forms and returns to scale
Determine profit-maximising output for competitive and monopoly firms
Use constrained optimisation, linear programming and input–output analysis on economic problems
Apply game theory and difference/differential equations to economic models
